speaker: Raquel Urtasun
title: An AI-First Approach to Enable Self Driving at Scale, with Raquel Urtasun of Waabi
question: In autonomous driving, what requirements must sensor simulation meet to reliably validate a self-driving stack in closed loop at scale?
guest: The last thing that we need to do is to be able to render the world with high fidelity and in real time. We do this through a combination of two things, which is physics as well as AI. The combination of these two things is very important because it enables you to have an unprecedented level of fidelity, and also it enables you to actually do this rendering in real time. This is key in order to be able to really use this at scale in closed-loop simulation. If your rendering takes hours or days, there is no way that you can really test the self-driving stack. What is important is that the output of the perception system is able to obtain the same results in the simulation as well as in the real world. This is the way that you can mathematically say that the perception system is seeing and reacting the same way in simulation as in the real world, so there is no need to observe a safety-critical occlusion scenario in the real world—we can just create that scenario in simulation and test whether the vehicle reacts.

points.core: Sensor rendering must run in real time rather than taking hours per scene.
points.note: Accept: real-time or near-real-time rendering speed is mandatory because slow multi-hour rendering makes large-scale closed-loop stack testing impossible. Do not credit: generic claims that faster compute is cheaper.

points.core: Combining physics models with AI achieves high sensor fidelity at real-time speed.
points.note: Accept: hybrid physics-plus-learned rendering bridges the tradeoff between accurate sensor realism and fast execution. Do not credit: naming a generic game engine without explaining the physics-AI fidelity-speed mechanism.

points.core: Simulated sensor inputs must produce the same perception outputs as real-world data.
points.note: Accept: sim-to-real correlation is validated when the perception system sees and reacts identically on simulated radar, lidar, or camera feeds as on real sensor logs. Do not credit: claiming images merely look visually photorealistic to humans.

points.core: Validated sensor simulation enables closed-loop testing of unseen safety-critical occlusion scenarios.
points.note: Accept: once sensor equivalence holds, teams can synthesize novel high-risk events like occluded vehicles encroaching without needing to encounter them on public roads. Do not credit: generic claims that simulation is safer than driving.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Sensor simulation for closed-loop validation has to satisfy several requirements at once.

First, it must be realistic enough that the domain gap is negligible: the autonomy stack should behave the same on simulated camera, lidar and radar data as on real data, including sensor-specific effects such as rolling shutter, lidar ray drop, noise, exposure and weather. This is best measured by downstream perception and planning agreement, not just visual quality.

Second, it must be reactive and controllable. Because the ego vehicle's actions change what it sees, the simulator must render novel viewpoints that deviate from recorded trajectories and allow actors to be edited, added or removed, with other agents behaving plausibly in response.

Third, it must be consistent: temporally, geometrically across sensors, and in timing, calibration and synchronization with the real sensor rig, as well as deterministic and repeatable.

Fourth, it must scale: fast and cheap enough to run millions of scenarios, with scenes built automatically from logs rather than hand-authored, and broad coverage of rare, safety-critical cases.

Finally, the simulator itself must be validated, showing that simulated outcomes statistically predict real-world performance.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: To reliably validate a self-driving stack in closed loop at scale, sensor simulation must bridge the sim-to-real gap while remaining reactive, deterministic, and computationally efficient. It requires high physical and perceptual fidelity across cameras, lidar, and radar—accurately modeling material reflectance, sensor noise, motion blur, rolling shutter, multipath returns, and adverse weather—so perception models behave as they do on real roads without exploiting synthetic artifacts. All modalities must maintain strict spatial alignment and tight temporal synchronization across frames. Because closed-loop evaluation lets the ego vehicle alter its trajectory while surrounding agents react dynamically, the simulator must synthesize plausible observations from novel viewpoints and counterfactual scene states without degradation. Scaling validation across millions of virtual miles further demands deterministic reproducibility, high throughput (including real-time execution when running hardware-in-the-loop), and automated generation of diverse, safety-critical edge cases. Finally, simulated sensor outputs must be quantitatively benchmarked against real-world logs to ensure virtual failure rates and system behaviors reliably predict on-road safety.

noweb.answer:
To reliably validate an autonomous driving stack in closed loop at scale, sensor simulation must first minimize the sim-to-real gap through high physical and perceptual fidelity across cameras, LiDAR, and radar. Rather than merely appearing realistic to humans, simulated outputs must capture sensor-specific physics and artifacts—such as rolling shutter, lens distortion, LiDAR beam divergence, radar multi-path reflections, and adverse weather degradations—so perception models behave identically to how they perform on real-world data. Multi-sensor streams must also maintain strict spatial calibration and temporal synchronization within a unified world state.

Because closed-loop validation allows the ego vehicle’s planner to deviate from recorded trajectories, the simulator must accurately render novel viewpoints and counterfactual interactions with reactive, dynamic agents without introducing geometric or appearance artifacts. Finally, operating at scale requires automated scene reconstruction, deterministic execution for reproducible debugging, and high computational throughput. Modern pipelines often combine physics-based rendering with neural reconstruction methods like 3D Gaussian splatting to rapidly turn real logs into editable environments and run millions of safety-critical virtual miles cost-effectively.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
For closed-loop validation at scale, sensor simulation has to do five things.

First, it needs high fidelity with a small domain gap. Camera, lidar and radar outputs must match real sensor physics and artifacts closely enough that perception behaves the same on simulated data as on real data. That includes noise, rolling shutter, motion blur, lens effects, weather, lighting, multipath and material reflectance. The test is whether the stack's errors match, not whether the images look good.

Second, it must be controllable and react to the vehicle. When the self-driving car departs from a logged trajectory, the simulator has to render new viewpoints and let other agents respond to it. Replaying logs can't do this, which is why neural reconstruction methods such as NeRF and Gaussian splatting are used alongside rule-based agent models.

Third, all sensors must be consistent with each other: synchronized in time, aligned in space and physically coherent.

Fourth, it must be deterministic and reproducible, so a regression can be traced to a specific code change.

Fifth, it must scale. That means rendering fast enough, or efficiently enough, to run millions of scenarios cheaply, including generated rare and edge cases.

Finally, the simulator itself has to be validated. Simulated and real results need to be compared quantitatively, and any remaining gap reported, so that sim results can count as safety evidence.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: To reliably validate a self-driving stack in closed loop at scale, sensor simulation must first minimize the sim-to-real gap across cameras, lidar, and radar by faithfully modeling optics, materials, weather, lighting, noise, and hardware artifacts such as rolling shutter or multipath reflections so perception networks respond as they would to real-world data. Outputs across all modalities must remain tightly calibrated and temporally synchronized. Because closed-loop evaluation lets the ego vehicle and surrounding road users diverge from logged trajectories, the simulator must render novel viewpoints and reactive dynamic actors on the fly while preserving geometric accuracy and temporal consistency across frames. Scaling to millions of miles and rare safety-critical edge cases further demands high rendering throughput, low compute cost, and automated scenario and asset generation from real driving logs or procedural worlds. Finally, the system must be deterministic for reproducible regression testing and quantitatively validated against real-world benchmarks to prove that simulated perception and driving behavior faithfully predict on-road performance.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Sensor simulation must deliver the same inputs the production stack expects, with realistic timing, calibration, and correlations across cameras, lidar, radar, and other sensors. It must reproduce the effects that can change driving decisions across the vehicle’s intended operating conditions, including occlusion, lighting, weather, motion distortion, noise, and sensor failures. Fidelity should be measured against real sensor recordings and real-world stack behavior using task-relevant metrics.

In closed loop, each control command must update the vehicle’s motion and the next sensor readings, while other road users can react to the vehicle. The simulation must preserve sensor rates, latency, and synchronization even when it runs faster or slower than wall-clock time.

At scale, it must run efficiently in parallel, vary conditions systematically, and cover rare, safety-critical scenarios. Versioned configurations, controlled randomness, and reproducible replay let teams diagnose failures and compare stack versions. Ground truth and consistent metrics make it possible to score perception and driving outcomes across runs.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Sensor simulation must reproduce what the stack’s cameras, lidar, radar, and other sensors would observe as the vehicle acts. Every steering or braking decision must change the vehicle’s pose and subsequent observations consistently across sensors. Other road users must respond plausibly when their interactions affect the outcome. Replaying a fixed sensor log cannot test this feedback loop.

Fidelity must be high enough to preserve the cues and errors that affect driving decisions. That includes geometry and occlusion, lighting and weather, sensor noise and missed detections, and the calibration, timing, and latency the deployed stack experiences. Real-world measurements should establish where the simulator reproduces sensor behavior and whether the stack responds similarly in matched scenarios. Visual realism alone cannot establish that.

At scale, the simulator must run enough repeatable, parallel trials to cover the intended operating conditions and rare safety-critical cases. It must preserve timing and fidelity at that throughput and let engineers reproduce failures.
